teile.einleitung: War crimes are serious breaches of the rules that apply even in war. These rules are called international humanitarian law. Above all, they are meant to protect civilians, the wounded and prisoners.
wichtigste: International humanitarian law applies even in war.
Article 8 of the Rome Statute lists the war crimes.
Starving civilians is a war crime.
Children under 15 must not be recruited into armed forces.
Every state party must prosecute or hand over people accused of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions.
In 2016 the International Criminal Court convicted al-Mahdi for destroying cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: Even in war, not everything is allowed. The **Geneva Conventions** of 1949 protect the wounded, prisoners and **civilians**. Switzerland is the **depositary state** of these conventions, meaning it keeps the originals. The **Rome Statute** of 1998 founded the **International Criminal Court** in The Hague. Its **Article 8** lists the war crimes in detail.

**Treachery**, also called **perfidy**, is forbidden. This means attacking by abusing the enemy's trust in protection, for example by pretending to be a civilian. Ordinary **ruses of war** such as camouflage are still allowed. **Starving** civilians is also a war crime, for example by blocking aid deliveries. It is equally forbidden to recruit **children under 15** into armed forces.

Particularly serious breaches of the Geneva Conventions are called **grave breaches**. They include, for example, wilful killing, torture or taking protected persons hostage. Every state party must **bring suspected offenders before its own courts or hand them over**. This applies regardless of their nationality. The aim is that offenders are safe nowhere.

**Cultural heritage** such as churches, mosques or monuments is also protected. In **2016** the International Criminal Court convicted **Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi**. In 2012 he had ordered the destruction of mausoleums and a mosque in **Timbuktu** in Mali. It was the Court's first case dealing only with the destruction of cultural heritage. Al-Mahdi was sentenced to 9 years in prison.

As early as the **American Civil War**, the US Army issued the **Lieber Code** in **1863**. With it, the lawyer **Francis Lieber** wrote down rules for the Union troops. They later influenced the **Hague Conventions**. After the First World War, the **Treaty of Versailles** of 1919 provided for charges against **Kaiser Wilhelm II**. However, the Netherlands, where he had fled, did not hand him over.

gewusst: The Red Cross and the Geneva Conventions have their origins in Switzerland.
The mausoleums of Timbuktu were rebuilt with the help of UNESCO after they were destroyed.

teile.einleitung: The Kyoto Protocol is an international treaty to protect the climate. It was agreed in 1997 in the Japanese city of Kyoto. For the first time, countries made a binding commitment to emit fewer greenhouse gases.
wichtigste: The aim of the Kyoto Protocol was to commit countries to reducing greenhouse gases.
The treaty was agreed in December 1997 at the climate conference in Kyoto.
It only came into force in February 2005.
From 2008 to 2012, industrialised countries were to cut their emissions by about 5 per cent on average compared with 1990.
The USA signed the treaty but never put it into force.
Switzerland committed itself to cutting its emissions by 8 per cent.
Its successor is the Paris Agreement of 2015.

abschnitte.text: The Kyoto Protocol is an additional treaty to the United Nations **Framework Convention on Climate Change** of 1992. That convention stated that global warming must be slowed down, but it contained no fixed figures. The Kyoto Protocol now set an exact **reduction commitment** for each industrialised country. This made climate protection a legal obligation for the first time.

abschnitte.titel: How it came about in Kyoto
abschnitte.text: In December 1997, experts and government representatives from more than 150 countries met in **Kyoto** in Japan. After long negotiations they agreed on the treaty on 11 December 1997. For it to take effect, enough countries had to ratify it, meaning have it confirmed by their own parliament. Only when Russia agreed in 2004 were enough countries on board, and the treaty came into force on **16 February 2005**.

The treaty covered six **greenhouse gases**, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. In the period from 2008 to 2012, industrialised countries were to cut their emissions by 5.2 per cent on average below the 1990 level. The European Union and Switzerland each promised minus 8 per cent. Developing countries such as China and India had no fixed targets, because at that time they emitted much less and were still meant to develop economically.

The protocol allowed so-called **flexible mechanisms**. A country that emitted less than allowed could sell its remaining rights to another country. This is called **emissions trading**. A country could also pay for climate projects in a poorer country, for example a solar power plant, and have the savings counted towards its own target.

Switzerland ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2003. To reach its target it relied on the **CO2 Act**, which has applied since 2000. Since 2008 there has been a CO2 levy on heating oil and natural gas, part of which is paid back to the population. Switzerland reached its target for 2008 to 2012, partly because it was allowed to count forests as CO2 stores and certificates from abroad.

Critics complained that big polluters such as the USA did not take part and that Canada pulled out again in 2011. In addition, worldwide emissions kept rising, mainly because China and other emerging economies grew strongly. In 2012 a second commitment period up to 2020 was agreed in Doha, but only a few countries took part. In 2015 came the **Paris Agreement**, in which almost all countries of the world set their own climate targets for the first time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that traps heat like the glass of a greenhouse, for example carbon dioxide.
A country officially confirms a treaty, usually through its parliament, and so makes it valid for itself.
A system in which rights to emit greenhouse gases can be bought and sold.
A yearly meeting of countries at which the protection of the climate is negotiated.

gewusst: More than seven years passed between the signing in Kyoto and the treaty coming into force.
Methane, one of the gases in the Kyoto Protocol, is also produced in the stomachs of cows.
The Kyoto climate conference was the third so-called Conference of the Parties, COP 3 for short.

teile.einleitung: In July 1995, more than 8000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in the area around Srebrenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina. International courts have classified the crime as genocide. It is regarded as the worst war crime in Europe since the Second World War.
wichtigste: The massacre happened in July 1995, during the Bosnian War.
More than 8000 Bosniak men and boys were murdered.
Dutch UN soldiers were supposed to protect the safe area but could not prevent the attack.
In 2007 the International Court of Justice found that Serbia had failed to prevent the genocide.
Ratko Mladić was sentenced to life imprisonment, partly because of Srebrenica.
The memorial and the cemetery of the victims are in Potočari.
Since 2024, 11 July has been an international UN day of remembrance.

abschnitte.text: After **Yugoslavia** broke apart, the **Bosnian War** took place from 1992 to 1995. In it, mainly Bosnian Serbs, Bosniaks and Croats fought each other. **Bosniaks** is the name for Bosnian Muslims. In 1993 the UN declared the town of **Srebrenica** in the east of the country a **safe area**. Many Bosniaks sought refuge there.

On 11 July 1995 **Bosnian Serb troops** took the enclave of Srebrenica. In the following days more than **8000 men and boys** were killed. The victims were buried in **mass graves**. Many could only be identified years later through **DNA analysis**. A lightly armed **Dutch battalion of UN peacekeepers** was stationed in the enclave. It could not prevent the attack.

The **Yugoslavia Tribunal** in The Hague prosecuted those responsible. The first to be found guilty of genocide, in 2001, was General **Radislav Krstić**. The army chief of the Bosnian Serbs, **Ratko Mladić**, was in hiding for years. He was arrested in 2011 and sentenced to **life imprisonment**, which was confirmed in 2021. In 2007 the **International Court of Justice** found that genocide had taken place in Srebrenica. Serbia was not found guilty of committing it, but it had breached its duty to prevent it.

In **Potočari** near Srebrenica are the central **memorial** and the cemetery of the victims. The UN troops' base used to be there. Every year on 11 July, newly identified victims are buried there. In 2024 the **UN General Assembly** declared 11 July an international day of remembrance. Serbia and Republika Srpska rejected the resolution.

gewusst: The Swiss lawyer Carla Del Ponte was chief prosecutor of the Yugoslavia Tribunal from 1999 to 2007.
Dutch courts later found the Dutch state partly responsible for the deaths of some of the victims.

teile.einleitung: Most-favoured-nation treatment is a basic principle of world trade. It says that a trade advantage a country grants to one partner must be granted to all partners. This way all members of the World Trade Organization (WTO) are meant to be treated equally.
wichtigste: If a WTO member lowers the customs duty for one country, this applies immediately to all members.
Most-favoured-nation treatment is set out in Article I of the GATT.
It applies unconditionally, meaning without anything in return.
Together with national treatment it forms the principle of non-discrimination.
Free trade areas and customs unions are a permitted exception.
Developing countries may receive lower customs duties.
Switzerland has been a full member of the GATT since 1966.

abschnitte.text: The term **most-favoured nation** sounds like a special privilege, but it actually means equal treatment. If a WTO member grants a country a lower **customs duty**, it must grant this advantage to all other members too. This must happen **immediately** and **unconditionally**. So the other members do not have to give anything in return. This prevents a country from treating its trading partners differently.

The **GATT** is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1947. Most-favoured-nation treatment appears right in **Article I**, which shows how important it is. **Article III** deals with **national treatment**: once imported goods have crossed the border, they must not be treated worse than domestic goods. Together, both rules form the **principle of non-discrimination**. Since 1995 the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, based in **Geneva**, has watched over these rules.

There are important exceptions. Under **Article XXIV** of the GATT, countries in **free trade areas** and **customs unions** may grant each other advantages without giving them to everyone. The condition is that essentially all trade between them becomes free. The **Enabling Clause** of 1979 allows rich countries to grant **developing countries** lower customs duties on a one-sided basis. Switzerland does this too with its **system of preferences**.

Switzerland joined the GATT provisionally in 1958 and definitively in **1966**. Since 1995 it has been a founding member of the **WTO**. As an exporting country, it benefits greatly from its goods being treated the same everywhere. In the USA, since 1998, most-favoured-nation treatment has mostly been called **“Normal Trade Relations”** in legal language. Congress chose this name because “most-favoured nation” wrongly sounded like a special privilege.

gewusst: Most-favoured-nation treatment is so important that it comes right at the start of the GATT, in Article I.
The World Trade Organization is based in Geneva, right on Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The Lok Sabha is the lower house of the Indian Parliament. It is elected directly by the people. Because India has so many voters, the election to the Lok Sabha is regarded as the largest democratic election in the world.
wichtigste: The name Lok Sabha means “House of the People”.
The second chamber is called the Rajya Sabha, “Council of States”.
543 members are elected by the people in constituencies.
Members are elected for five years, and you can vote from the age of 18.
You can stand for the Lok Sabha from the age of 25.
The 2024 election lasted about six weeks.
The Lok Sabha meets in New Delhi.

abschnitte.text: The Indian Parliament has two chambers, similar to the Swiss Parliament. The **Lok Sabha** is the **lower house**. “Lok” means people, “Sabha” means assembly or house. The second chamber is the **Rajya Sabha**, the **upper house**. It represents India's states, just as the Council of States in Switzerland represents the cantons.

India is divided into **543 constituencies**. In each constituency exactly one member of the Lok Sabha is elected. Whoever gets the most votes wins the seat. You can vote from the age of **18**. Anyone who wants to be elected must be at least **25 years** old. The Lok Sabha is elected for **five years**, unless it is dissolved earlier.

The last election took place in 2024. It lasted from 19 April to 1 June, about **six weeks**. Voting took place in **seven phases**, one after another in different parts of the country. The reason is the huge number of almost one billion voters. This way, election workers and security forces can be deployed step by step all over the country. Votes are usually cast on **electronic voting machines**.

The Lok Sabha passes **laws** together with the Rajya Sabha. It also decides on the **national budget**, in other words what the state spends money on. The **prime minister** needs the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha. If the government loses this majority, it can be brought down. The sittings are chaired by a **Speaker**, the president of the chamber.

The Indian Parliament is based in the capital, **New Delhi**. Since 2023 it has met in a **new parliament building**. The old, round building dates from the time when India was a British colony. India has been independent since 1947. The first Lok Sabha was elected at the beginning of the 1950s.

gewusst: Because of its huge number of voters, India is regarded as the largest democracy in the world.
For the election, polling stations are set up even in very remote places so that everyone can vote.

teile.einleitung: Media such as newspapers, radio, television and social networks report on what is happening in politics. They influence what people think about and how they vote. At the same time they keep a check on those in power, which makes them very important for a democracy like Switzerland.
wichtigste: The media are often called the “Fourth Estate” because they keep a check on government, parliament and the courts.
According to agenda-setting theory, the media decide which topics the public thinks about.
With framing, the media place a topic in a particular frame of interpretation through selection and emphasis.
The spiral of silence theory says that people tend to keep quiet about their opinion if they think they are in the minority.
The term “filter bubble” was coined by Eli Pariser in 2011.
Article 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship.
The Swiss Press Council judges complaints about breaches of the journalists' code.

abschnitte.text: In a democracy, power is divided between three branches: parliament, government and the courts. The media are often called the **Fourth Estate** because they watch over and keep a check on these three. Journalists uncover abuses, waste or bribery, for example. Without free media, citizens could hardly know what the authorities are doing. In Switzerland in particular, with its many **popular votes**, people need good information to be able to decide.

In 1972 the researchers Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw showed with their **agenda-setting** theory that the media decide what we think about. What often appears on the front page is seen by many people as especially important. **Framing** is about how a topic is presented. Whether you speak of “tax relief” or “loss of revenue”, for example, stirs up very different feelings. So the same news can have a different effect depending on its frame.

abschnitte.titel: Spiral of silence and filter bubble
abschnitte.text: In 1974 the German researcher Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann described the **spiral of silence**. Anyone who believes their opinion is in the minority is more likely to keep quiet, and so the other opinion seems even stronger. On the internet there is also the **filter bubble**, a term Eli Pariser made famous in 2011 with his book of the same name. Algorithms of search engines and social networks mostly show us what fits our previous clicks. As a result, we see other opinions less often.

Article 17 of the **Federal Constitution** guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship. So the state may not dictate what newspapers or broadcasters report. The **SRG SSR** offers radio and television programmes in all four national languages and is mainly funded by a fee paid by households and businesses. In 2018 the No Billag initiative wanted to abolish these fees, but it was clearly rejected, with about 72 per cent voting no.

Journalists in Switzerland follow a **journalists' code** with duties and rights. This includes reporting truthfully, checking facts and respecting people's privacy. Anyone who thinks a report breaks these rules can complain to the **Swiss Press Council**. The Press Council judges the case and publishes its opinion, but it does not impose penalties.

Always check who is behind a news item and whether reliable sources report the same thing. False reports, also called **fake news**, often spread especially quickly on social networks. On important topics, read reports from different media to get to know several points of view. Also pay attention to whether a text is a news report or a comment giving a personal opinion.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the state forbids or controls what may be published.
The way a topic is presented so that people understand it in a particular way.
A set of calculation instructions that a computer program uses, for example, to choose which posts you see.
A body that checks whether the media are following the rules of good journalism.

gewusst: The Swiss Press Council was founded in 1977 and is supported by journalists' associations and publishers.
The SRG broadcasts programmes in German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The term “Fourth Estate” is unofficial, because the constitution only has three branches of power.

t1avp14i.t: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development

teile.einleitung: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development is known as UNCTAD for short. It works to make sure that poorer countries also benefit from world trade. It is based in Geneva.
wichtigste: The first UNCTAD conference took place in Geneva in 1964.
The first Secretary-General was the Argentinian Raúl Prebisch.
The Group of 77 developing countries was formed there in 1964.
In 1968 the Generalised System of Preferences was agreed.
UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report every year.
Together with the WTO it runs the International Trade Centre in Geneva.
Since 2021 Rebeca Grynspan has led UNCTAD as the first woman in the role (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: The first **UNCTAD conference** met in **Geneva** in **1964**. It led to a permanent body of the **UN General Assembly**. Many countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America had just become independent at that time. They wanted the rules of world trade to benefit them as well. UNCTAD is still based in Geneva today.

The first Secretary-General was the Argentinian **Raúl Prebisch**, from 1964 to 1969. Together with Hans Singer he put forward the **Prebisch-Singer thesis**. It says that in the long run the prices of **raw materials** fall compared with those of **manufactured goods**. Countries that mainly sell raw materials therefore fall behind. This is why UNCTAD called for industrialisation and trade advantages for developing countries.

At the first conference, **77 developing countries** signed a joint declaration. This is how the **Group of 77**, or G77 for short, came about. Today more than 130 countries belong to it, but the name has stayed. Together the countries carry more weight at the UN.

abschnitte.titel: Lower customs duties for poorer countries
abschnitte.text: At the conference in **New Delhi** in **1968**, the **Generalised System of Preferences** was agreed. Under it, industrialised countries grant developing countries **lower customs duties** on a one-sided basis. This makes it easier for them to sell their goods. **Switzerland** also uses such a system.

Every year UNCTAD publishes the **World Investment Report**. It shows how much money flows into other countries worldwide as **direct investment**. Together with the **WTO**, UNCTAD runs the **International Trade Centre** (ITC) in Geneva. It helps small and medium-sized firms in developing countries to export. Since **2021** UNCTAD has been led by **Rebeca Grynspan** from Costa Rica (as of 2025).

gewusst: Geneva is an important place for world trade, because UNCTAD, the WTO and the International Trade Centre are all based there.
The World Trade Report is published not by UNCTAD but by the WTO.

teile.einleitung: The Copenhagen criteria set out the conditions a country must meet to join the EU. The European Council agreed them in Copenhagen in June 1993. They still apply today.
wichtigste: The criteria were laid down in Copenhagen in 1993.
Politically, democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the protection of minorities are required.
Economically, a functioning market economy is required.
A country that wants to join must adopt the acquis communautaire.
The EU itself must also be able to take in new members.
The accession procedure is set out in Article 49 of the EU Treaty.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the Cold War, many countries in **Central and Eastern Europe** wanted to join the EU. In **June 1993** the **European Council** decided in **Copenhagen** which conditions they had to meet. Since then these rules have been called the **Copenhagen criteria**. They apply to all countries that want to become members today.

A candidate country needs **stable institutions**. They must guarantee **democracy**, the **rule of law** and **human rights**. The **protection of minorities** is also named explicitly. These values also appear in **Article 2** of the EU Treaty, together with human dignity. Respecting them is a condition for applying.

The country needs a **functioning market economy**. Its companies must be able to cope with **competitive pressure** in the single market. In the single market there are no customs duties between members. So the economy must be strong enough to keep up with the competition.

A candidate country must adopt the **acquis communautaire**. This is the entire body of EU law: treaties, laws, court rulings and agreements. The **accession negotiations** are divided into **chapters**, for example on agriculture or the environment. In **1995** the European Council in **Madrid** also stressed that candidates need an administration able to apply EU law effectively.

abschnitte.titel: The EU must be ready too
abschnitte.text: The Copenhagen Council named one more condition for the EU itself. It must be able to **take in new members** without losing momentum. This **capacity to absorb** new members is often called the fourth criterion. The procedure is governed by **Article 49** of the EU Treaty. The Council must decide **unanimously**, and the European Parliament must give its consent.

gewusst: Under Article 49, only a European state can apply for membership.
Switzerland is not a member of the EU; it organises its relations through bilateral agreements.

teile.einleitung: At the San Francisco Conference in 1945, the Charter of the United Nations was drawn up. Representatives of 50 countries negotiated for about two months. This founded the UN.
wichtigste: The conference began on 25 April 1945.
Representatives of 50 countries took part.
Poland was absent but still became a founding member.
The UN was prepared in 1944 at Dumbarton Oaks and in 1945 at Yalta.
President Roosevelt died shortly before the conference began.
The plenary sessions were held in the San Francisco opera house.
China was the first country to sign the Charter.

abschnitte.text: Even during the **Second World War**, the Allies were planning a new world organisation. In **1944** the USA, Great Britain, the Soviet Union and China drew up its basic structure at **Dumbarton Oaks** near Washington. In **February 1945** the “Big Three”, **Roosevelt**, **Churchill** and **Stalin**, met at **Yalta** in Crimea. There they decided to hold the founding conference in San Francisco in April.

US President **Franklin D. Roosevelt** had pushed hard for the founding of the UN. However, he died on **12 April 1945**, shortly before the conference began. His successor **Harry S. Truman** carried the project forward. The conference began as planned on **25 April 1945**. In the Pacific, the war was still going on at that time.

The official name of the meeting was the **“United Nations Conference on International Organization”**, or **UNCIO** for short. Representatives of **50 countries** negotiated for about two months. The large plenary sessions were held in the **War Memorial Opera House**, the city's opera house. Many other meetings took place in committees.

At the end, the **UN Charter** was signed. **China** was allowed to sign first. It had been the first country to be attacked by an Axis power, namely by Japan in **1937**. **Poland** had not been invited because of a dispute over its government. It signed in October 1945 and counts as one of the **51 founding members**.

**Switzerland** was not present in San Francisco. It stayed outside the UN for a long time, partly because of its **neutrality**. Even so, **Geneva** became an important UN location in Europe. Switzerland only joined the UN after a **popular vote in 2002**. Today almost every country in the world belongs to the UN.

gewusst: The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, which is why this day is United Nations Day.
In 2002 Switzerland became the 190th member of the UN.

teile.einleitung: Mediation means helping to settle a dispute. A neutral person helps the people in conflict to find a solution themselves. In world politics Switzerland is known for its mediation.
wichtigste: In mediation, a neutral third party helps the sides find a solution themselves.
All parties to the conflict must agree to the mediation.
As a neutral country, Switzerland offers its “good offices”.
In 2009 Armenia and Turkey signed protocols in Zurich that Switzerland had mediated.
On the Bürgenstock, talks were held about the Nuba Mountains in 2002 and about Cyprus in 2004.
Within the FDFA, the Peace and Human Rights Division is responsible for mediation.

abschnitte.text: In **mediation**, a neutral person, the **mediator**, supports the talks between two sides. The mediator does not decide who is right. The **parties to the conflict** must find and accept the solution themselves. What matters is that everyone involved agrees. Nobody can be forced into mediation. Many schools also have peer mediators who work in this way.

Switzerland is **neutral** and does not belong to any military alliance. That is why both sides of a conflict often trust it. It offers its **good offices**: it provides places for negotiations or mediates itself. Many international organisations are based in **Geneva**, and peace talks often take place there. In the **FDFA**, the foreign ministry, the **Peace and Human Rights Division** is responsible for promoting peace.

The **Bürgenstock**, high above Lake Lucerne, has several times been the setting for important talks. In January 2002 Switzerland and the USA made talks about the **Nuba Mountains** in Sudan possible there. A **ceasefire** was agreed. In March 2004 the reunification of the island of **Cyprus** was negotiated on the Bürgenstock. The UN plan later failed in a referendum on the island.

On 10 October 2009 **Armenia** and **Turkey** signed protocols in **Zurich** to improve their relations. Switzerland had accompanied the talks. In 2011 it mediated between **Russia** and **Georgia**, so that Russia was able to join the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2012. In **Mozambique**, the Swiss diplomat **Mirko Manzoni** helped with the talks between the government and the opposition. A peace agreement was signed there in 2019.

gewusst: Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran as a so-called protecting power.
The word mediation comes from the Latin word for “middle”: the mediator stands in the middle between the parties.

teile.einleitung: Martin Luther King was an American minister and the best-known leader of the civil rights movement. He fought without violence for Black people in the USA to have the same rights as white people. His speech “I Have a Dream” is world-famous.
wichtigste: Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta in 1929.
In 1963 he gave the speech “I Have a Dream” in front of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington.
His model for non-violent resistance was Mahatma Gandhi.
In 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned racial segregation in public places.
In 1965 he marched from Selma to Montgomery for the right to vote.
In 1968 he was murdered in Memphis.

abschnitte.text: Martin Luther King was born on 15 January 1929 in **Atlanta** in the state of Georgia. His father was a minister, and Martin also became a **Baptist minister**. At that time there was **racial segregation** in the southern states of the USA. Black people were not allowed to use the same schools, restaurants or bus seats as white people. King wanted to end this injustice.

King's great role model was **Mahatma Gandhi**, who had led India to independence without violence. In 1959 King travelled to India to learn more about him. He relied on **non-violent** methods such as boycotts, marches and sit-ins. He became known in 1955 during the **Montgomery bus boycott**. It began after Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat to a white man.

On 28 August 1963, during the **March on Washington**, King gave his famous speech **“I Have a Dream”**. He stood in front of the **Lincoln Memorial**, the monument to Abraham Lincoln. The place was well chosen, because Lincoln stands for the end of slavery. In the speech King dreamed of a country in which all people are treated equally. In 1964, at the age of 35, he received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

The civil rights movement achieved important laws. The **Civil Rights Act** of 1964 banned discrimination in restaurants, hotels and at work. But many Black people were still prevented by tricks from registering as voters. So in 1965 King led the **march from Selma to Montgomery**. After that Congress passed the **Voting Rights Act**, which protected the right to vote.

On 4 April 1968 Martin Luther King was shot dead in **Memphis**. He was there to support striking refuse workers. His death caused great grief. Since 1986 **Martin Luther King Day** has been a public holiday in the USA. It falls on the third Monday in January, close to his birthday.

gewusst: Martin Luther King and his father were named after the German reformer Martin Luther.
When he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, he was the youngest winner up to that time.

teile.einleitung: Liechtenstein is a small principality between Switzerland and Austria. It is closely linked to Switzerland: people pay in francs there and speak German. At the head of the country is a prince.
wichtigste: Liechtenstein borders only Switzerland and Austria.
The Rhine forms the border with the canton of St Gallen.
People pay in Swiss francs and speak German.
The country is only about 160 square kilometres in size and has 11 municipalities.
The capital is Vaduz, and the highest mountain is the Grauspitz at 2599 metres.
The parliament, the Landtag, has 25 members.

abschnitte.text: Liechtenstein lies in the **Rhine Valley**. In the west it borders Switzerland, in the east Austria. The **Rhine** forms the border with the canton of **St Gallen**. In the south it borders the canton of the **Grisons**. At about **160 square kilometres** it is one of the smallest countries in the world, even smaller than the canton of Zug. The highest mountain is the **Grauspitz** at 2599 metres.

Liechtenstein is a **monarchy**: its head of state is a **prince**. At the same time there is a parliament, the **Landtag**, with 25 members. Of these, 15 come from the **Oberland** (upper country) and 10 from the **Unterland** (lower country). As in Switzerland, the people can also vote on some questions. Above the capital **Vaduz** stands **Vaduz Castle**, the home of the princely family.

Liechtenstein has only **11 municipalities**. They include **Vaduz**, where the government and parliament have their seat, as well as **Schaan** and **Balzers**. The official language is **German**. In everyday life people speak an Alemannic dialect that sounds similar to the one in the St Gallen Rhine Valley.

Liechtenstein has no currency of its own. For more than 100 years people there have paid in **Swiss francs**. Since a **customs treaty** of 1923 there has also been no customs border between the two countries. The border with Switzerland is open, and you hardly notice when you cross it. Unlike Switzerland, Liechtenstein is a member of the **European Economic Area (EEA)**. It joined the UN as early as 1990.

The flag of Liechtenstein has two horizontal stripes: **blue** at the top and **red** at the bottom. In the top left there is a golden **crown**. It stands for the bond between the people and the princely house. The crown was added in 1937, because before that the flag looked exactly the same as that of Haiti.

gewusst: Liechtenstein is a doubly landlocked country: its neighbours Switzerland and Austria have no sea either.
At the 1936 Olympic Games it was noticed that Liechtenstein and Haiti had almost the same flag.

teile.einleitung: The Millennium Development Goals were eight UN goals against poverty, hunger and disease. They were agreed in 2000 and were to be reached by 2015. After that they were replaced by the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
wichtigste: There were eight Millennium Development Goals.
189 countries adopted the Millennium Declaration in September 2000.
The goals were to be reached by 2015, compared with 1990.
Goal 1 aimed to halve the proportion of people in extreme poverty.
Goal 2 called for primary education for all children.
Goal 8 was aimed mainly at the rich countries.
In 2015 they were replaced by the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

abschnitte.text: In September 2000, heads of state and government met at the UN **Millennium Summit** in **New York**. On 9 September, 189 member states adopted the **Millennium Declaration**. The **eight Millennium Development Goals** were drawn from it. They were to be reached by **2015**. The year of comparison was usually **1990**.

**Goal 1** aimed to halve extreme poverty and hunger. **Goal 2** called for all girls and boys to be able to complete **primary school**. Goal 3 promoted equality between women and men. **Goal 4** called for cutting the death rate of children under five by **two thirds**. Goal 5 concerned the health of mothers. **Goal 6** was aimed at **HIV/AIDS**, malaria and other serious diseases. Goal 7 concerned protecting the environment, and **Goal 8** a global partnership.

abschnitte.titel: The task of the rich countries
abschnitte.text: Most of the goals concerned mainly the **developing countries**. **Goal 8**, however, was aimed at the **rich countries**. They were to give more development aid, create fairer trade rules and cancel the **debts** of poor countries. Switzerland also supported the goals, mainly through the **SDC**, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation.

According to the UN report of 2015, the number of people in extreme poverty fell from about **1.9 billion** to about **836 million**. A large part of the progress came from **China** and **India**. The number of deaths among children under five fell by about half. So the target of two thirds was not quite reached. In addition, much of the progress was unevenly spread.

In 2015 the **17 Sustainable Development Goals** replaced the Millennium Goals. They are part of the **2030 Agenda** and are to be reached by 2030. Unlike the Millennium Goals, they apply to all countries, including the rich ones. Besides poverty and education, they also deal with climate, energy and cities.

gewusst: The Millennium Goals got their name because they were agreed at the turn of the millennium in 2000.
Between 1990 and 2015 the number of people in extreme poverty fell by more than half.

teile.einleitung: A crown is a precious ornament worn on the head. It shows that someone rules a country, for example a king or a queen. Crowns are usually made of gold and decorated with precious stones.
wichtigste: A king or queen wears the crown on their head.
Crowns are usually made of gold or silver.
Precious stones such as diamonds, rubies and sapphires sparkle on crowns.
A crown is usually a ring with points or arches.
The crown is a sign of power.
The British Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London.

abschnitte.text: A **crown** is an ornament that you put on your **head**. Usually it is a **band**, in other words a ring, with **points** or **arches**. That way it fits nicely on the head. Some crowns are closed at the top, others are open. There is often soft fabric inside so that it sits more comfortably.

Crowns are usually made of **gold** or **silver**. These metals shine beautifully and are valuable. On top of that come **precious stones** such as **diamonds**, **rubies** and **sapphires**. Pearls are often seen too. That is why crowns are among the most valuable objects in the world.

The crown is a **sign of power**. Whoever wears it is a **king**, **queen** or **emperor**. At a **coronation**, the crown is ceremonially placed on the head of a new ruler. In everyday life, however, kings hardly ever wear their crown. It is only used at special celebrations.

In **Great Britain** there are the famous **Crown Jewels**. They include crowns, sceptres and other treasures. They are kept under close guard in the **Tower of London**, an old castle on the **Thames**. Visitors can see them there. King **Charles III** was crowned with one of these crowns in May 2023.

**Switzerland** has no king and no crown. It is a **republic** in which the people have a say. Here you only see crowns in a **museum** or at carnival time. On **Epiphany** (Three Kings' Day) in January, though, there is the **Three Kings' cake**. Whoever finds the hidden little figure may wear a paper crown and is king for a day.

gewusst: In Denmark, Norway and Sweden the money is called the “krone” or “krona”, which means crown.
The Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire dates from the Middle Ages and is now kept in Vienna.

t1n38m0p.t: Member states of the United Nations

teile.einleitung: The United Nations (UN) has 193 member states. Almost every country in the world belongs to it. Switzerland has been a member since 2002, the first country to join as a result of a popular vote.
wichtigste: The UN has 193 member states.
The most recent member is South Sudan, since 2011.
Vatican City is not a member, only an observer.
Liechtenstein has been a member since 1990, Austria since 1955.
Switzerland joined in 2002 after a popular vote.
In the General Assembly each country has one vote.
Most members come from Africa.

abschnitte.text: The UN was founded in 1945, with 51 members at the time. According to the **UN Charter**, **peace-loving states** can become members. For a country to join, the **Security Council** and the **General Assembly** must agree. Today the UN has **193 members**. Most of them come from **Africa**: all 54 African countries belong to it.

In the **General Assembly**, each member country has exactly **one vote**. It makes no difference whether a country is large or small. So Switzerland counts just as much as China. Things are different in the **Security Council**: there, five permanent members have a right of veto. With it, each of them can block decisions on its own.

**Austria** became fully independent again in 1955 and joined the UN in the same year. In 1973 the two German states, **West and East Germany**, became members at the same time. **Liechtenstein** joined as early as **1990**, twelve years before Switzerland. Small states such as San Marino and Monaco are full members too. **Vatican City**, on the other hand, is only an **observer**, as is Palestine.

Switzerland had worked with the UN for a long time, and an important UN office is in **Geneva**. But it only became a member late. In 1986 the people still clearly rejected joining. On **3 March 2002** the **people and the cantons** said yes. Switzerland was the first country to join as a result of a **popular vote**. In September 2002 it became the 190th member.

The most recent member is **South Sudan**. It became a separate country in 2011 and shortly afterwards the **193rd member**. There was a special case with **Indonesia**: in January 1965 it announced it was leaving in protest. In 1966, however, it resumed its participation. The UN treated this only as a temporary interruption.

gewusst: In front of the UN headquarters in New York fly the flags of all the member states.
Shortly after Switzerland, East Timor also joined the UN in 2002.

teile.einleitung: The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty to protect the ozone layer. It bans substances such as CFCs that destroy ozone. It is regarded as one of the most successful environmental agreements in the world.
wichtigste: The Montreal Protocol was signed on 16 September 1987.
It came into force on 1 January 1989.
It mainly regulates CFCs, which used to be found in spray cans and fridges.
The ozone layer protects us from the sun's UV radiation.
The ozone hole was discovered over Antarctica in the 1980s.
By 2009 all UN member states had ratified the protocol.
Ozone has been measured in Arosa since 1926.

abschnitte.text: **Ozone** is a gas made of three oxygen particles. About 90 per cent of ozone is in the **stratosphere**, about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground. This **ozone layer** acts like a filter. It holds back a large part of the sun's **UV radiation**. Too much UV radiation causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer.

Certain substances destroy ozone, above all **CFCs**, **chlorofluorocarbons**. They used to be found in spray cans, fridges and foams. In 1985 British researchers reported a strong thinning of the ozone layer over **Antarctica**. It is called the **ozone hole**. It appears there every year in the southern hemisphere's spring. The researchers **Paul Crutzen**, **Mario Molina** and **Sherwood Rowland** had explained how ozone is broken down, and for this they received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1995.

The **Montreal Protocol** was signed on **16 September 1987** in Montreal in Canada. It came into force on **1 January 1989** and was later tightened several times. The production of CFCs was banned step by step. By 2009 all UN member states had ratified the protocol, the last being East Timor. No UN treaty had managed this before. Today 16 September is the **International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer**.

**Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs)** were often used to replace CFCs. They do not harm ozone, but they are very powerful **greenhouse gases**. That is why the protocol was extended in 2016 with the **Kigali Amendment**. It restricts these substances too. In this way the Montreal Protocol also helps the climate today.

In **Arosa** in the Grisons, the researcher **Paul Götz** began measuring ozone in 1926. Measurements have been taken there ever since, for longer than anywhere else in the world. Today **MeteoSwiss** continues this longest ozone measurement series in the world. The measurements show how the ozone layer has changed over decades. Experts expect the ozone layer to recover over the coming decades thanks to the protocol.

gewusst: The Montreal Protocol was the first UN treaty to be ratified by truly every member state.
The ozone measurement series from Arosa is the longest in the whole world.

teile.einleitung: The Overland Transport Agreement is a treaty between Switzerland and the European Union. It governs the movement of lorries and trains across borders. It is part of the Bilateral Agreements I.
wichtigste: The agreement is part of the Bilaterals I and has applied since 2002.
Since then, lorries in Switzerland may weigh up to 40 tonnes; before, it was 28 tonnes.
Since 2001 heavy lorries have paid the HVF for every kilometre driven.
Switzerland wants to shift goods from road to rail.
The Alpine Initiative was accepted in 1994.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in 2016.
The night-time and Sunday driving ban for lorries still applies.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is not a member of the EU; it organises its relations through **bilateral agreements**. The **Overland Transport Agreement** is part of the **Bilaterals I** package of seven agreements. It was signed in 1999. In 2000 the Swiss people approved the Bilaterals I. The agreement has been in force since 2002.

In the past, lorries in Switzerland could weigh at most **28 tonnes**, while in the EU the limit was 40 tonnes. With the agreement the limit was raised step by step to **40 tonnes**. In return the EU recognised the **heavy vehicle fee (HVF)**, which is based on performance. It has been charged since 1 January 2001. How much a lorry pays depends on its weight, the kilometres driven and its emissions standard. Part of the money goes into expanding the railways.

Switzerland wants to move as much **transit traffic** through the Alps as possible onto the railways. This is called **modal shift** from road to rail. Its basis is the **Alpine Initiative**, which was accepted on 20 February 1994. Since then, protecting the Alpine region from transit traffic has been written into the **Federal Constitution**. This protects the environment and the people from noise and exhaust fumes.

So that more goods travel by train, Switzerland built the **New Rail Link through the Alps (NRLA)**. It includes the **Lötschberg Base Tunnel**, which opened in 2007. In June 2016 the **Gotthard Base Tunnel** followed, about 57 kilometres long. In 2020 the Ceneri Base Tunnel in Ticino was added. Freight trains can now travel through the Alps on flatter routes and more quickly.

Switzerland was able to keep some of its own rules. The **night-time and Sunday driving ban** for lorries still applies; it protects people from noise. There is also a **ban on cabotage**. Cabotage means transporting goods from one place to another within a foreign country. So a lorry from the EU may not deliver goods from Basel to Zurich.

gewusst: At about 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
In Switzerland lorries are banned from driving at night from 10 pm to 5 am.

t1ru5n16.t: List of the countries of the world

teile.einleitung: There are about 195 countries on Earth. However, the exact number cannot be given, because not all countries are recognised everywhere. The countries vary greatly in size and are spread unevenly across the continents.
wichtigste: Usually about 195 countries are counted.
They include the 193 UN members, Vatican City and Palestine.
With 54 countries, Africa has the most.
There are no countries in Antarctica.
Since 2023 India has had more inhabitants than China.
South Sudan has been independent since 2011 and is regarded as the youngest country.
Australia takes up almost an entire continent.

abschnitte.text: Usually about **195 countries** are counted. They include the **193 members of the UN** as well as **Vatican City** and **Palestine**, which are observers at the UN. Some territories such as **Kosovo** or **Taiwan** are recognised as separate countries by only some states. Switzerland, for example, has recognised Kosovo since 2008. That is why people usually say “about 195”.

**Africa** has 54 countries, more than any other continent. **Asia** is larger, but has fewer countries. In **Antarctica**, at the South Pole, there are no countries, only research stations. An international treaty ensures that it is used peacefully for research. **Australia** is a special case: the whole mainland belongs to a single country, plus the island of Tasmania.

The largest country in the world by area is **Russia**. In America, **Canada** is the largest; it is even slightly bigger than the USA. The smallest country in the world is **Vatican City**, in the middle of Rome. **Monaco** is tiny too, only about 2 square kilometres. With just over 41,000 square kilometres, Switzerland lies somewhere in between.

**India** has the most inhabitants. In 2023 it overtook **China**. Both countries have more than 1.4 billion people. Together, more than a third of all the people in the world live there. Vatican City has the fewest inhabitants, with only a few hundred people.

The number of countries changes over time. After the Second World War many former **colonies** became independent, especially in Africa and Asia. When the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia broke apart, new countries also came into being. The youngest generally recognised country is **South Sudan**. It separated from Sudan in 2011 and became a member of the UN.

gewusst: Russia is so large that it stretches across eleven time zones.
Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre and lies entirely within the city of Rome.

teile.einleitung: A microcredit is a very small loan for people who cannot get money from a normal bank. With it they can start a small business, for example. The idea became famous through the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.
wichtigste: Microcredits are small loans, often only a few hundred dollars.
Poor people often cannot get a loan from normal banks because they have no collateral.
Most of the Grameen Bank's loans go to women.
Many borrowers form small groups that support each other.
The UN declared 2005 the International Year of Microcredit.
Critics warn of high interest rates and excessive debt.
In 2001 BlueOrchard, one of the first investment funds for microfinance, was set up in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: A **microcredit** is a small loan, often only a few hundred dollars. It is aimed at poor people who cannot get a loan from normal banks. Banks usually ask for **collateral** such as land or a house, which these people do not have. In addition, the administrative costs of very small amounts are high in relation to the loan. With a microcredit, someone can buy a sewing machine, chickens or goods for a market stall, for example.

The best-known microcredit bank is the **Grameen Bank** in **Bangladesh**. “Grameen” comes from Bengali and means something like “village” or “rural”. It was founded by the economics professor **Muhammad Yunus**. Most of its borrowers are **women**; in 2007 they made up about 97 per cent. Women are seen as especially reliable and often invest in the family. In 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

Many microcredits are given to **solidarity groups**. The borrowers join together in small groups and support each other. Only when the first members repay regularly do others receive a loan. In this way, trust within the group replaces the missing collateral. The term **microfinance** is broader: it also includes savings accounts, insurance and money transfers for people on low incomes.

Microcredits are not without controversy. The **interest rates** are often more than 20 per cent a year. Some borrowers take out new loans to pay off old ones and fall into a **debt trap**. Around 2010 there was a crisis in the Indian state of **Andhra Pradesh** because of massive **over-indebtedness**. The government then placed tight restrictions on microfinance institutions.

The UN declared **2005** the **International Year of Microcredit**. It saw microcredit as a way to fight poverty. Switzerland plays a role too: in 2001 **BlueOrchard**, one of the first commercial investment funds for microfinance, was set up in **Geneva**. It invests investors' money in microfinance institutions in many countries. Switzerland is regarded as an important centre for such investments.

gewusst: In the 1970s Muhammad Yunus gave his first loans out of his own pocket to women in a village.
The Grameen Bank is largely owned by its own borrowers.

teile.einleitung: Malala Yousafzai is a campaigner for girls' right to education. She comes from Pakistan and became world-famous as a teenager. In 2014 she became the youngest person ever to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Malala grew up in the Swat Valley in northern Pakistan.
She campaigns above all for girls' education.
In October 2012 she was shot by the Taliban on her way to school.
She was treated in Birmingham in England.
In 2013 her book “I Am Malala” was published.
In 2014 she received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Kailash Satyarthi.
In 2020 she completed her degree at Oxford.

abschnitte.text: Malala Yousafzai was born in 1997 in the **Swat Valley** in northern **Pakistan**. Her father ran a school and supported her greatly. In her region the **Taliban** took power for a time. They banned girls from going to school. But Malala was determined to keep learning.

Even as a child, Malala wrote a **diary** on the internet. In it she described how important school was to her. She also gave interviews and demanded the **right to education** for all girls. This made her well known in Pakistan. For the Taliban it was a provocation.

In October **2012** a Taliban fighter shot Malala on the school bus. She was seriously injured but survived. She was flown to **Birmingham** in England and treated in a hospital that specialises in serious injuries. Her family then moved to England as well. The attack caused outrage around the world.

In 2013 her book **“I Am Malala”** was published, which she wrote with the journalist Christina Lamb. In 2014, at the age of 17, she received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. She shared it with the Indian **Kailash Satyarthi**, who fights against child labour. In this way the Nobel Committee honoured a Muslim woman from Pakistan and a Hindu from India together. Both work for children.

Malala studied philosophy, politics and economics at the University of **Oxford**. She graduated in 2020. With her father she founded the **Malala Fund**. This organisation supports education projects for girls in many countries. Malala gives speeches all over the world, including at the UN.

gewusst: Malala is the youngest person ever to have received a Nobel Prize.
On her 16th birthday in 2013, Malala gave a speech at the UN in New York.

teile.einleitung: The Kosovo War was a war in 1998 and 1999 over the region of Kosovo in South-East Europe. It ended after 78 days of NATO air strikes. Afterwards Kosovo came under international administration.
wichtigste: The NATO air strikes were called Operation Allied Force.
They lasted from 24 March to 10 June 1999, which is 78 days.
Before that, the Rambouillet negotiations had failed.
The operation was controversial because there was no mandate from the UN Security Council.
Resolution 1244 placed Kosovo under international administration.
Switzerland takes part in KFOR with Swisscoy.
For the German armed forces it was the first combat mission since 1945.

abschnitte.text: At that time **Kosovo** belonged to **Serbia**, which together with Montenegro formed the **Federal Republic of Yugoslavia**. The majority of the population were **Kosovo Albanians**. They wanted more self-government or independence. From 1998 the Albanian group **KLA** (UÇK) and Serbian security forces fought each other. Many people had to flee.

In **February and March 1999**, talks were held at the **Château de Rambouillet** near Paris. The aim was an agreement on **autonomy** for Kosovo, meaning extensive self-government. The Yugoslav side rejected the draft. **NATO** then decided to intervene militarily.

On **24 March 1999**, NATO began **Operation Allied Force**. Its aircraft attacked military and strategic targets in Serbia and Kosovo. The attacks ended on **10 June 1999**, after **78 days**. For the German **Bundeswehr** it was the **first combat mission** since the Second World War. It took part with Tornado aircraft.

The operation lacked a **mandate from the UN Security Council**. Russia and China would have blocked such a mandate. Supporters spoke of a **humanitarian intervention** to protect the population. Critics saw it as a breach of the **ban on the use of force** in international law. This question is still debated today.

**Resolution 1244** of 10 June 1999 placed Kosovo under the **UN interim administration UNMIK**. The international security force **KFOR** was to keep the peace. Since 1999 **Switzerland** has taken part with **Swisscoy**, which is made up of volunteers. In 2008 Kosovo declared its independence, which not all countries recognise.

gewusst: Swisscoy is the Swiss Army's largest mission abroad to promote peace.
Resolution 1244 is still in force today.

teile.einleitung: The War Material Act governs whether Swiss companies may sell weapons and ammunition abroad. It is meant to stop Swiss war material from reaching conflict zones. Since the war in Ukraine it has been the subject of fierce debate.
wichtigste: Licences are granted by SECO, together with the FDFA.
As a rule, nothing is delivered to countries involved in an armed conflict.
With a non-re-export declaration, buyers promise not to pass anything on without permission.
In 2022 Germany was not allowed to pass Swiss ammunition for the Gepard on to Ukraine.
Denmark was not allowed to pass on Piranha armoured vehicles either.
In 2009 the people rejected an export ban, with 68.2 per cent voting no.
Since 1 May 2022 the licensing criteria have been set out in the act itself.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, exporting **war material** requires a **licence**. Applications are examined by the **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs** (SECO) together with the **FDFA**. Difficult cases are decided by the **Federal Council**. As a rule, exports are ruled out if the receiving country is involved in an **armed conflict**. On top of this comes the **principle of equal treatment** under the law of neutrality.

Anyone who buys Swiss war material often signs a **non-re-export declaration**. With it, the buying country promises **not to pass the material on** to third parties **without Switzerland's consent**. This is meant to stop weapons from reaching conflict zones by roundabout routes. This rule became especially important after Russia attacked Ukraine.

**Germany** had supplied Ukraine with **Gepard** anti-aircraft tanks. It wanted to pass on Swiss **35-millimetre ammunition** for them. It had originally been developed by **Oerlikon**. Switzerland refused in 2022. **Denmark** was not allowed to pass **Piranha** wheeled armoured personnel carriers made by the firm **Mowag** from Kreuzlingen on to Ukraine either.

On **29 November 2009** the people voted on a **ban on exports of war material**. **68.2 per cent** said no, and all the cantons rejected it too. Later came the **“Correction Initiative”**, which wanted stricter rules. Its counter-proposal came into force on **1 May 2022**: the licensing criteria are now set out in the **act** instead of an ordinance. This means Parliament decides on changes, and the initiators withdrew their initiative.

abschnitte.titel: The dispute over relaxing the rules
abschnitte.text: The **arms industry** warns about the strict rules. It fears that foreign customers will no longer buy Swiss parts if they are not allowed to pass them on in an emergency. This, it says, puts jobs and the country's own defence industry at risk. Others stress **neutrality** and protection against supplying weapons to wars. Since then, Parliament has been debating whether to relax the rules.

gewusst: The Gepard has two cannons and its own radar to detect aircraft.
The firm Mowag in Kreuzlingen also supplies Piranha vehicles to the Swiss Army.

teile.einleitung: Thailand is a kingdom in South-East Asia. At the head of the state is a king, while a prime minister leads the government. The king is deeply revered in Thailand.
wichtigste: Thailand is a monarchy and its head of state is a king.
Maha Vajiralongkorn has been king since 2016; he is also called Rama X.
His father Bhumibol reigned from 1946 to 2016, about 70 years.
The capital is Bangkok, where the Grand Palace stands.
Thailand used to be called Siam.
In cinemas, people stand up when the royal anthem is played.

abschnitte.titel: A king as head of state
abschnitte.text: Thailand is a **constitutional monarchy**. This means there is a king, but also a constitution, a parliament and a government. Until 1932 the king held all the power; then the **absolute monarchy** was abolished. Today the government is led by a **prime minister**. The king is seen as a symbol of the country's unity. Criticising the king is forbidden in Thailand by strict laws and can be punished severely.

Today's royal family is called the **Chakri dynasty** and has ruled since 1782. Its kings also carry the title **Rama** with a number. The number shows which king of the family it is. Today's king, **Maha Vajiralongkorn**, is Rama X, the tenth. He became king in 2016 and was formally crowned in 2019.

King **Bhumibol** reigned from 1946 to 2016, a total of 70 years. He was one of the rulers who sat on a throne the longest. In his youth he lived in Switzerland for a long time, in **Lausanne**. There he went to school and studied at the university. Many Thai people revered him deeply. After his death the whole country mourned for a year.

**Bangkok** is the capital and the largest city in Thailand. It is home to the **Grand Palace**, which was built from 1782 onwards. For a long time it was where the kings lived. Today it is used mainly for ceremonies and visited by many tourists. Within the palace grounds there is also a famous temple with the **Emerald Buddha**.

For a long time the country was called **Siam**. The name **Thailand** was introduced in 1939 and has been final since 1949. It means something like “land of the free”. The word **Siamese cat**, for example, comes from the old name. In the cinema, the **royal anthem** is often played before the film, and everyone stands up out of respect.

gewusst: Thailand was never ruled as a colony by a European power.
King Bhumibol spent a large part of his youth in Lausanne on Lake Geneva.

t9voif9.t: Member states of the European Union

teile.einleitung: The European Union (EU) is an association of European countries. Since Great Britain left in 2020, it has had 27 members. Switzerland does not belong to it, but it is surrounded by EU countries.
wichtigste: Since 2020 the EU has had 27 member states.
The European Economic Community was founded by six countries in 1957.
Germany has the most inhabitants, France the largest area.
Malta is the smallest member, both by area and by population.
In 2004 ten countries joined at once.
Luxembourg is the only grand duchy in the world.
Switzerland organises its relations with the EU through bilateral agreements.

abschnitte.text: The history of the EU begins after the Second World War. In 1957 six countries signed the **Treaties of Rome** and founded the **European Economic Community**. The founders were **Belgium**, **Germany**, **France**, **Italy**, **Luxembourg** and the **Netherlands**. They wanted to secure peace through cooperation. This later developed into the European Union.

Gradually more countries joined. The largest **enlargement** took place on 1 May **2004**: ten countries joined at once, including **Poland** and the **Czech Republic**. Most of them came from Central and Eastern Europe, along with **Malta** and **Cyprus**. The most recent country to join was **Croatia** in 2013. In 2020 **Great Britain** left the EU, and since then it has had **27 members**.

**Germany** has more than 80 million inhabitants and is the EU country with the largest population. **France** is the largest by area, followed by Spain and Sweden. The smallest member is the island state of **Malta**, with only about 316 square kilometres. **Luxembourg** is a **grand duchy**, with a Grand Duke at its head. Other EU countries are monarchies too, such as Spain, Belgium or Sweden.

**Cyprus** lies in the eastern Mediterranean and joined the EU in 2004. The island is divided: since 1974 the north has been controlled by **Turkey**. In practice EU law does not apply there. The UN has been working for decades to reunite the island. So far this has not succeeded.

Four of Switzerland's neighbours are in the EU: **Germany**, **France**, **Italy** and **Austria**. Switzerland itself is not a member. In 1992 the people narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area. Since then Switzerland has organised its relations through **bilateral agreements**, for example on the **free movement of persons** or on **Schengen**. This gives it access to the **single market** in certain areas.

gewusst: Malta is just under half the size of the canton of Glarus and is still a full EU member.
Great Britain is so far the only country to have left the EU again.

teile.einleitung: A supply chain covers all the steps a product goes through, from raw material to customer. Today companies from many countries are often involved. If one link in the chain fails, people all over the world feel it.
wichtigste: A supply chain includes extracting raw materials, manufacturing, transport and sale.
Many goods travel in containers, measured in TEU, the size of a 20-foot container.
With just-in-time, parts are delivered exactly when they are needed.
In March 2021 the “Ever Given” blocked the Suez Canal for six days.
In 2021 and 2022 there was a worldwide shortage of computer chips, which slowed down the car industry.
Cargo ships reach as far as Basel via the Rhine.
The Responsible Business Initiative failed in 2020 because it did not win a majority of the cantons.

abschnitte.text: A **supply chain** shows the path of a product. It begins with a **raw material**, for example cocoa, cotton or ore. This is then processed, assembled into a product, transported and sold. A mobile phone is made of parts from many different countries. That is why people often speak of **global supply chains**.

A large part of world trade travels on **container ships**. Containers come in standard sizes and fit on ships, trains and lorries. Cargo is measured in **TEU**, which stands for “Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit”. This means a container **20 feet** long, about 6 metres. Switzerland is connected to the sea via the **Rhine**: cargo ships travel up to the **Swiss Rhine Ports** in Basel.

Many factories work on the **just-in-time** principle. Parts are delivered exactly when they are needed. This means the factory hardly needs a warehouse and saves money. But if a delivery fails, production quickly comes to a standstill. This method became well known mainly through the Japanese carmaker Toyota.

In March 2021 the huge container ship **“Ever Given”** ran aground in the **Suez Canal**. It blocked the canal for six days, and hundreds of ships were stuck in a queue. During the **coronavirus pandemic**, **computer chips** (semiconductors) became scarce. In 2021 and 2022 many car factories therefore had to stop production at times. Disruptions like these show how strongly countries depend on one another.

Supply chains can involve problems such as **child labour** or environmental damage. The **Responsible Business Initiative** wanted to make Swiss companies liable for this. On 29 November 2020 it won a narrow majority of the votes. However, most cantons rejected it, so it failed because it did not win the **majority of the cantons**. After that, a counter-proposal by Parliament came into force which, among other things, requires large companies to publish reports.

gewusst: The largest container ships can carry more than 20,000 containers at once.
The Responsible Business Initiative was one of the few initiatives that won a majority of the people and still failed.

teile.einleitung: Mercosur is an association of countries in South America. It is meant to make trade between its members easier. The name means “Common Market of the South”.
wichtigste: Mercosur was founded in 1991 with the Treaty of Asunción.
Its founders were Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Venezuela has been suspended since 2016.
Bolivia became a full member in 2024.
Chile is only an associate member.
The main languages are Spanish and Portuguese.
Brazil has the largest economy in Mercosur.

abschnitte.text: **Mercosur** is short for **Mercado Común del Sur**. “Mercado” means market, “común” common and “sur” south. In Portuguese the organisation is called **Mercosul**. The aim is for goods, services and people to cross borders more easily. The secretariat is based in **Montevideo**, the capital of Uruguay.

On 26 March 1991, **Argentina**, **Brazil**, **Paraguay** and **Uruguay** signed the **Treaty of Asunción**. It is named after the capital of Paraguay, where it was signed. In 1994 the **Protocol of Ouro Preto** followed. It gave Mercosur its own **legal personality** and set up its bodies. From 1995 there was also a **customs union** with a common **external tariff** towards other countries.

**Venezuela** became a member in 2012 but was **suspended** in December 2016 because it did not keep to the bloc's rules. **Bolivia** signed the accession protocol in 2015 and became a full member in 2024. This means Mercosur has five active full members. **Chile** and other South American countries are only **associate members**. They cooperate, but they are not part of the customs union.

In **Brazil** people speak **Portuguese**, in the other member countries mainly **Spanish**. In Paraguay the indigenous language **Guaraní** is also widely spoken. Brazil is the largest country in South America by area and by population. Its economy is bigger than those of all the other members put together. Important exports of Mercosur include soya, meat and ore.

Mercosur also negotiates **free trade** with other parts of the world. **EFTA**, to which Switzerland belongs, concluded negotiations on a free trade agreement with Mercosur in 2025. The **European Union** also negotiated such an agreement for many years. In Europe this is controversial: supporters expect more trade, while critics worry about farming and the rainforest.

gewusst: Mercosur's founding treaty is named after Asunción, the capital of Paraguay.
Brazil is so large that it borders almost all the other countries of South America.

teile.einleitung: A coronation is a solemn ceremony in which a new king or queen has the crown placed on their head. It shows everyone that the country now has a new head. Coronations in Great Britain are especially well known.
wichtigste: At a coronation, the crown is ceremonially placed on a new ruler's head.
British kings and queens have been crowned in Westminster Abbey in London for almost 1000 years.
The Archbishop of Canterbury places the crown on the British king's head.
King Charles III was crowned on 6 May 2023.
The king travels to the coronation in a magnificent horse-drawn coach.
Afterwards the royal family waves from the balcony of Buckingham Palace.
The coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953 was broadcast on television.

abschnitte.text: A **coronation** is the solemn start of the reign of a king or queen. The **crown** is a sign of power and dignity. Other symbols often go with it, for example a **sceptre** (a decorated rod) and an **orb** (a ball with a cross). In the past many people believed that a king received his power from God. That is why coronations usually took place in a church.

In Great Britain, coronations take place in **Westminster Abbey**, a large, old church in London. The ceremony is led by the **Archbishop of Canterbury**, the senior clergyman of the Church of England. The king sits on an ancient coronation chair. He takes an oath and promises to serve the country. A particularly solemn moment is the **anointing** with holy oil. Only after that is the crown placed on his head.

The king travels to the coronation in a magnificent **coach** pulled by horses. Soldiers in colourful uniforms accompany the procession through the streets. Many people line the roads and cheer. After the ceremony the royal family appears on the **balcony of Buckingham Palace**. Thousands of people wait below and wave back.

Queen **Elizabeth II** was crowned on 2 June 1953. Her coronation was broadcast on **television**, and millions of people watched. Many families bought a television set especially for it. Her son **Charles III** was crowned on 6 May 2023. His wife Camilla was crowned queen together with him.

Not all monarchies crown their rulers. In Spain, Denmark or the Netherlands there is no longer a coronation; there the new king takes office with a ceremony or an oath. In the Middle Ages emperors were crowned too: **Charlemagne** was crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome in the year 800. Switzerland is a republic and has no king, so there are no coronations here.

gewusst: In 1804 in Paris, Napoleon placed the imperial crown on his own head, even though the Pope was present.
The British Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London and can be visited.

teile.einleitung: There are still about a dozen monarchies in Europe today. In them a king, a queen or a prince is at the head of the state. Almost everywhere, parliament holds the real power.
wichtigste: Liechtenstein, our neighbour, is a principality.
Felipe VI has been King of Spain since 2014.
Frederik X has been King of Denmark since January 2024.
Since August 2026 Haakon VIII has been King of Norway.
Philippe has been King of the Belgians since 2013.
Willem-Alexander has been King of the Netherlands since 2013.
Sweden has a king; Germany, Italy and Austria are republics.

abschnitte.text: The kingdoms in Europe are **Belgium**, **Denmark**, the **Netherlands**, **Norway**, **Sweden**, **Spain** and the **United Kingdom**. In addition there are the principalities of **Liechtenstein** and **Monaco** and the Grand Duchy of **Luxembourg**. **Andorra** and **Vatican City** also have a special form of monarchy. Our neighbouring countries **Germany**, **Italy**, **France** and **Austria**, on the other hand, are republics. Almost all monarchies in Europe are **parliamentary monarchies**.

**Felipe VI** has been King of **Spain** since 2014. He succeeded his father **Juan Carlos**, who abdicated. **Philippe** has been King of the **Belgians** since 2013. His title is deliberately “King of the Belgians” and not “King of Belgium”. Belgium lies between France and the Netherlands.

**Willem-Alexander** has been King of the **Netherlands** since 2013. He succeeded his mother Beatrix, who abdicated. He lives in **The Hague**, where the government and parliament also sit. The royal family is called the **House of Orange**. That is why on **King's Day** on 27 April many people wear **orange** clothes and celebrate in the streets.

In **Sweden**, **Carl XVI Gustaf** has been king since 1973. **Frederik X** became King of **Denmark** in January 2024, after his mother Margrethe II abdicated. In **Norway**, King **Harald V** died in August 2026. His son **Haakon** became the new king and is now called **Haakon VIII**. In all three countries the king mainly has ceremonial duties.

Switzerland's neighbour with a prince is **Liechtenstein**. It lies between Switzerland and Austria. Unlike in most monarchies, the prince there still has quite a lot of political power. **Monaco** on the Mediterranean is also a principality, ruled by the Grimaldi family. And in **Luxembourg** a **Grand Duke** is at the head of the state.

gewusst: In Sweden, since 1980, the eldest child becomes heir to the throne, whether a girl or a boy.
Andorra has two heads of state: the French president and a Spanish bishop.

teile.einleitung: The Kurds are a people with their own language and culture who live in the Middle East. They are often described as the largest people without a state of their own. The Kurdish conflict is about their rights, their self-government and the question of a state of their own.
wichtigste: The area where Kurds live lies mainly in Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria.
Most Kurds live in Turkey.
The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 made no provision for a Kurdish state.
Abdullah Öcalan founded the PKK in 1978, which fought against the Turkish state from 1984.
In northern Iraq there is an Autonomous Kurdistan Region with its capital Erbil.
In 1988 the town of Halabja was attacked with poison gas.
In May 2025 the PKK announced that it would dissolve.

abschnitte.text: The area where many Kurds live is called **Kurdistan**. It is not a state; it stretches across **Turkey**, **Iraq**, **Iran** and **Syria**. The Kurds speak **Kurdish** and have their own traditions. An important festival is **Newroz**, the New Year festival in spring. Many Kurds now also live in Europe, including Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Treaties after the First World War
abschnitte.text: After the First World War, the Ottoman Empire broke apart. The **Treaty of Sèvres** of 1920 still held out the prospect of self-government for the Kurds. But it was never put into effect. In 1923 it was replaced by the **Treaty of Lausanne**, which was signed in the Swiss city of Lausanne. It fixed the borders of present-day Turkey and no longer mentioned a Kurdish state.

In Turkey, Kurds were for a long time not allowed to use their language freely. In 1978 **Abdullah Öcalan** founded the **Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK)**. From 1984 it waged an armed struggle against the Turkish state in which many people died. Turkey, the EU and the USA classify the PKK as a terrorist organisation. Öcalan was captured in Kenya in 1999 and has been held on the prison island of İmralı ever since. In May 2025, following his call, the PKK announced its **dissolution** and the end of its armed struggle.

Under the dictator **Saddam Hussein**, the Kurds in Iraq were severely persecuted. In the **poison gas attack on Halabja** in March 1988, several thousand civilians died. Today northern Iraq has the **Autonomous Kurdistan Region** with its own government and parliament in **Erbil**. Its self-government is set out in the Iraqi constitution of 2005. In a **referendum** in September 2017, more than 90 per cent voted for independence. The Iraqi government and most countries rejected the result, and it was not put into effect.

In the **Syrian civil war**, Kurdish groups took control of areas in the north of the country. There they also fought against the terrorist militia “Islamic State”. Many Kurds also live in **Iran**, mainly in the west of the country. There too, Kurdish groups are demanding more rights. The governments of the countries concerned, on the other hand, want to preserve their borders and their unity.

gewusst: The borders of present-day Turkey were fixed in Switzerland in 1923, in the Treaty of Lausanne.
