The Kurdish New Year festival Newroz is celebrated on 21 March, at the start of spring.

teile.einleitung: With the cohesion contribution, Switzerland supports poorer member states of the EU. The money goes into projects meant to reduce differences within Europe. It used to be called the enlargement contribution.
wichtigste: Its basis is the Eastern Europe Cooperation Act, accepted in 2006 with about 53 per cent.
The first contribution came to about 1.3 billion francs in total.
Poland received the largest share.
The SDC and SECO carry out the projects.
The money goes into projects, not into the EU budget.
The Switzerland-EU package plans 350 million francs per year for 2030 to 2036.

abschnitte.text: **Cohesion** means holding together. In the EU there are richer and poorer regions. Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it has access to its **single market**. With the contribution it helps to reduce the **economic and social differences** in Europe. This also strengthens its relations with the EU.

The basis is the **Federal Act on Cooperation with the States of Eastern Europe**, known as the Eastern Europe Cooperation Act. A **referendum** was launched against it. On **26 November 2006** the people accepted the act with **53.4 per cent** voting yes. This allowed Switzerland to make the contribution.

At first **1 billion francs** was planned for the ten countries that had joined the EU in **2004**. Later, contributions for **Bulgaria**, **Romania** and **Croatia** were added. In total it came to about **1.3 billion francs**. **Poland**, the new member with the largest population, received the biggest share. Projects in transport, the environment and research, for example, were supported.

Switzerland does **not pay the contribution into the EU budget**. It funds **specific projects** that it agrees on with the partner countries. The **Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation** (SDC) and the **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs** (SECO) look after them. For the part on migration, the State Secretariat for Migration is also involved.

In the **Switzerland-EU package**, the contribution is to be made **legally binding** for the first time. It will be set for **seven years** at a time, matching the EU's financial framework. For the years **2030 to 2036**, **350 million francs per year** are planned. The package is the subject of political debate in Switzerland, as supporters and opponents judge it very differently.

gewusst: Switzerland decides together with the partner countries which projects it supports.
In the EU enlargement of 2004, Poland was the largest new member.

teile.einleitung: Every year many people from Africa and Asia try to reach Europe across the Mediterranean. Several routes are distinguished. The crossing in boats that are often overcrowded is very dangerous.
wichtigste: There is a western, a central and an eastern Mediterranean route.
The central route runs mainly from Libya and Tunisia to Italy.
The small island of Lampedusa is often the first place people arrive.
The central route is regarded as the deadliest.
The western route runs from Morocco to Spain, the eastern route from Turkey to Greece.
The border agency Frontex is based in Warsaw.
In 2022 Swiss voters approved a higher contribution to Frontex.

abschnitte.text: Three main routes across the Mediterranean are distinguished. The **western route** runs from **Morocco** to **Spain**, across the Strait of Gibraltar or to the Spanish territories of **Ceuta** and **Melilla** in North Africa. The **central route** runs from **Libya** or **Tunisia** to **Italy**. The **eastern route** runs from **Turkey** to Greek islands in the Aegean. There the distance is in places only a few kilometres.

The small Italian island of **Lampedusa** is closer to Africa than to the Italian mainland. That is why many boats arrive there. Many set off from **Libya**, where there has been great insecurity since Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011. **Smugglers** take advantage of this and demand a lot of money for the crossing. The route is long and the boats are often overcrowded. According to the **International Organization for Migration**, more people die on this route than on any other.

In October 2013 a boat capsized off Lampedusa and more than 360 people died. After that the **Italian navy** launched Operation **“Mare Nostrum”**. Within a year it rescued a great many people in distress at sea. Today private aid organisations also operate rescue ships. How sea rescue should be organised is politically disputed in Europe.

The European border agency **Frontex** was founded in 2004 and is based in **Warsaw**. It helps countries protect the **external borders of the Schengen area**. Switzerland is a member of Schengen and therefore takes part in Frontex. In May 2022 Swiss voters approved an increase in the contribution, with about **71 per cent** in favour. Supporters stressed security, while opponents criticised the way refugees are treated.

On the Greek island of **Lesbos** there was the **Moria** camp. It had been built for far fewer people, but at times more than 12,000 people lived there in cramped conditions. In September 2020 the camp burned down. The residents lost their shelter. The fire sparked debates across Europe about taking in refugees.

gewusst: Lampedusa is closer to Tunisia than to Sicily.
Between the Turkish coast and some Greek islands there are only about ten kilometres of sea.

teile.einleitung: The territorial sea is the strip of sea directly off a country's coast. There, the sea belongs to the country almost as much as the land itself. The rules for it are set out in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
wichtigste: The territorial sea is at most 12 nautical miles wide, which is about 22 kilometres.
It is measured from the baseline, usually the low-water line along the coast.
The country has sovereignty over the water, the seabed and the airspace.
Foreign ships have the right of innocent passage.
Harbours and bays behind the baseline are internal waters.
The contiguous zone reaches up to 24 nautical miles, for example for customs and immigration.

abschnitte.text: The **territorial sea** is also called territorial waters. It reaches at most **12 nautical miles** out to sea. A nautical mile measures 1852 metres, so 12 nautical miles are about 22 kilometres. In this strip the coastal state exercises its **sovereignty**. It covers the water, the seabed, the ground beneath it and the **airspace** above it.

The territorial sea is measured from the **baseline**. The normal baseline follows the **low-water line**, the line at low tide. On very jagged coasts with many bays and islands, straight lines may be drawn between certain points. Everything on the land side of the baseline, such as harbours and bays, counts as **internal waters**. They are fully part of the country's territory.

Foreign ships may pass through the territorial sea. This is called the **right of innocent passage**. However, the ships must not disturb the peace and security of the coastal state. They are not allowed to fish or extract raw materials there. In internal waters this right of passage does not exist as a rule.

abschnitte.titel: From the cannon to 12 nautical miles
abschnitte.text: In the past the **cannon-shot rule** applied: the sea belonged to the country as far as a cannon could fire from the shore. That was about three nautical miles. Later many countries demanded wider zones. The **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea** of 1982 set the limit at 12 nautical miles. The convention came into force in 1994.

Directly beyond the territorial sea lies the **contiguous zone**, which reaches up to 24 nautical miles. There the country may, for example, enforce customs and immigration rules and pursue smugglers. The **exclusive economic zone** reaches up to 200 nautical miles; only the coastal state may fish and use raw materials there. Beyond that begin the **high seas**, which are open to all countries.

gewusst: Although Switzerland has no sea, there are ocean-going ships under the Swiss flag with Basel as their home port.
A nautical mile is as long as one minute of arc on a meridian of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: A consulate is a smaller mission of a country that helps its citizens abroad. It deals with passports, emergencies and questions from people who live or travel abroad. Unlike an embassy, it is often not in the capital.
wichtigste: A consulate helps its own citizens abroad.
An embassy mainly represents a country towards the government of the host country.
Consulates issue passports and identity cards, for example.
They help in emergencies such as accidents, theft or arrest.
The rules are set out in the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations of 1963.
A consulate general is a larger consulate.
An honorary consul works for a country on a voluntary basis.

abschnitte.text: A **consulate** is an office of a country in a city abroad. It is there mainly for people, not for government politics. The person in charge is called the **consul**. Larger consulates are called consulates general. A country can have several consulates in different cities of another country.

An **embassy** is usually in the capital and represents the country towards the government. The ambassador works there. A consulate, on the other hand, deals with practical questions from citizens. An embassy often has a consular section too. Switzerland, for example, has an embassy in Rome and a consulate general in Milan.

A consulate issues **passports** and identity cards. It reports births, marriages and deaths abroad to the home country. It helps when someone has an accident, is robbed or is arrested abroad. For foreigners who want to enter the country, it often issues visas. It also supports companies and encourages contacts in culture and business.

The tasks and rights of consulates are set out in the **Vienna Convention** on Consular Relations of 1963. It says, for example, that a consulate may visit an arrested person from its country. The premises of a consulate are specially protected. The police of the host country may only enter them with permission. Consuls enjoy a certain protection, but less than diplomats in an embassy.

More than 800,000 Swiss people live abroad. For them and for travellers, the Swiss missions are important places to turn to. The foreign ministry, the FDFA, also runs a **helpline** that can be reached around the clock. Before a trip you can register with the Travel Admin app. Voluntary honorary consuls help in places where there is no embassy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who runs a consulate.
Permission to enter a foreign country.
A person who represents a country in a city on a voluntary basis.
Swiss people who live permanently in another country.

gewusst: The word consul comes from ancient Rome, where the consuls were the highest officials of the state.
Many honorary consuls are business people who work for another country alongside their job.

teile.einleitung: A monarchy is a form of state in which a king, a queen or a prince is at the head of the country. The office is usually passed down within the family. Switzerland is not a monarchy but a republic.
wichtigste: In a monarchy, a king, a queen or a prince is the head of state.
A country with a king or queen is called a kingdom.
Usually a child of the king inherits the office; this is called a hereditary monarchy.
A king usually reigns until his death.
A king is addressed as “Majesty”.
In Great Britain, Parliament makes the laws, not the king.
Switzerland has no king; it is a republic.

abschnitte.text: The word **monarchy** comes from Greek and means “rule by one person”. At the head is a **monarch**: a king, a queen, a prince or an emperor. A country with a king or a queen is called a **kingdom**, for example Spain or Denmark. A country with a prince is called a **principality**, like Liechtenstein. A king's wife is usually called the **queen**, and together they are the **royal couple**.

Usually you are born into the royal family. A child of the king or queen later inherits the office. That is why it is called a **hereditary monarchy**. The person who will be the next king is called the **heir to the throne**. A king usually reigns for life, until his death. But some give up the office voluntarily in old age; this is called **abdication**.

In the past many kings held all the power; this is called an **absolute monarchy**. Today most monarchies in Europe are **parliamentary monarchies**. There the king has little power. In **Great Britain**, for example, **Parliament** passes the laws and an elected government runs the country. The king mainly represents the country at ceremonies and state visits.

Kings and queens are addressed as **“Your Majesty”**. This is an old, very polite form of address. For princes, the German-speaking world uses the title **“Durchlaucht”**, which corresponds to “Serene Highness”. A monarchy often also includes a crown, a sceptre and magnificent palaces. Many people are interested in the lives of royal families.

Switzerland has **no king**. It is a **republic**. The people elect the parliament and can vote themselves on many questions. Instead of a king there is the **Federal Council** with seven members who govern together. Interestingly, the famous ruling family of the **Habsburgs** originally came from the area of today's Switzerland; their ancestral castle stands in the canton of Aargau.

gewusst: The Pope is the head of Vatican City and is elected, not born into the role: an elective monarchy.
Habsburg Castle in the canton of Aargau is the ancestral seat of one of the most powerful ruling families in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Since April 2023 there has been war in Sudan. The army and the RSF militia are fighting for power in the country. Millions of people have had to flee, and many are suffering from hunger.
wichtigste: Since April 2023 the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been fighting.
The army is led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the RSF by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.
The RSF grew out of the Janjaweed militias.
The ruler Omar al-Bashir was overthrown in 2019.
Sudan has the largest displacement crisis in the world (as of 2025).
The army government moved its seat to Port Sudan.

abschnitte.text: **Omar al-Bashir** had ruled Sudan since **1989**. The **International Criminal Court** wanted him for crimes in Darfur. After large **protests**, the military removed him in **April 2019**. After that the country was meant to move towards democracy. In 2021, however, the army and the RSF carried out a coup together.

In **April 2023** the two sides began fighting each other. The **army** is led by **Abdel Fattah al-Burhan**. The **Rapid Support Forces** (RSF) militia is led by **Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo**, known as **Hemedti**. Both want power in the country. Because of the fighting in the capital **Khartoum**, the army government moved its seat to **Port Sudan** on the Red Sea.

The RSF grew out of the **Janjaweed** militias. From 2003 these were involved in serious crimes during the **Darfur conflict**. Under al-Bashir they were reorganised as the RSF in 2013. In **Darfur**, in the west of the country, the population is again badly affected by violence. In October 2025 the RSF captured the city of **El Fasher**, the army's last major stronghold in Darfur.

According to the UN, more than **12 million people** have been displaced (as of 2025). This makes Sudan the **largest displacement crisis in the world**. Many fled to neighbouring countries such as **Chad**, **Egypt** and **South Sudan**. In August 2024 an expert panel declared a **famine** in the **Zamzam** camp near El Fasher. Sieges and blocked aid deliveries are seen as the main causes.

Other countries also play a role. Experts and UN reports often accuse the **United Arab Emirates** of supplying the RSF with weapons. The Emirates deny this. Aid organisations are calling for the fighting to stop and for aid to be allowed through to the people.

gewusst: South Sudan has been a separate country since 2011; its capital is Juba.
In Khartoum the White Nile and the Blue Nile flow together.

teile.einleitung: Consular protection is the help a country gives its citizens abroad. For Switzerland, embassies and consulates of the FDFA take care of this. They help in emergencies, but not with everything.
wichtigste: If you lose your passport abroad, you contact the Swiss embassy or consulate.
The mission can issue a provisional passport.
People who are arrested have the right to contact their consulate.
The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations dates from 1963.
Honorary consuls work on a voluntary basis and often live in the host country.
You have to pay fines abroad yourself.
Before travelling it is worth looking at the FDFA's travel advice.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has **missions** in many countries. The **embassy** mainly looks after political relations with the host country. The **consulate** takes care of citizens, for example with identity documents or emergencies. Often both tasks are combined in the same building. In Switzerland the responsible body is the **FDFA**, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.

If you lose your **passport** abroad or it is stolen, you report to the Swiss **embassy** or **consulate**. The mission can issue a **provisional passport**. With it you can continue your journey or return home. However, it is only valid for a short time. It is also best to report a theft to the local police.

The rules for consulates are set out in the **Vienna Convention on Consular Relations** of **1963**. It governs the tasks and rights of consulates. **Article 36** is important: if a foreigner is **arrested**, the authorities must tell them that they can have their consulate informed. Consular officials may then visit them.

There is not a separate embassy everywhere. In that case **honorary consuls** often help. They are usually respected local people who work for a country on a **voluntary basis**. They often live in the host country and know their way around well. Switzerland has many such **honorary representations**.

Abroad, the principle of **personal responsibility** applies. The embassy helps in real emergencies. But it does not pay **fines**, bail or lawyers' fees. Anyone who travels should prepare well. In its **travel advice**, the FDFA gives information about dangers such as unrest, crime or natural hazards.

gewusst: The FDFA runs a helpline that can be reached around the clock.
Even in countries where Switzerland has no mission, an honorary consul can often help.

teile.einleitung: The Sahel is a dry belt south of the Sahara. Since 2012, violence by armed groups has been spreading there. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger are especially affected.
wichtigste: The Sahel lies between the Sahara Desert and the savannah.
The crisis began in Mali in 2012.
From 2014 to 2022 France fought terrorist groups with Operation Barkhane.
The UN mission MINUSMA left Mali at the end of 2023.
In 2023 Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger founded the Alliance of Sahel States.
Russia became Mali's most important security partner.

abschnitte.text: The **Sahel** stretches from the **Atlantic** to the **Red Sea**. It lies between the **Sahara** Desert in the north and the savannah in the south. The climate is dry and there are often **droughts**. Countries such as **Mali**, **Burkina Faso** and **Niger** suffer from poverty. On top of that, there has been violence by armed groups for years.

In **2012** the **Tuareg** rebelled in the north of Mali. After that, **jihadist groups** took over large areas. These are armed groups that pursue their aims with violence and in the name of a radical interpretation of Islam. From Mali the violence spread to Burkina Faso and Niger. One important group is **JNIM**, which is linked to **al-Qaeda**.

**France** intervened in Mali in 2013 with Operation **Serval**. From **2014** it extended the mission to the whole Sahel as Operation **Barkhane**. After tensions with the new military governments, Barkhane ended in **2022**. The UN had been in Mali since 2013 with the **MINUSMA** mission, one of the most dangerous UN missions. At the request of the military government it ended at the **end of 2023**.

In **Mali**, **Burkina Faso** and **Niger**, the military took power in coups. In **2023** the three countries founded the **Alliance of Sahel States** (AES). At the start of 2025 they left the West African economic community **ECOWAS**. From the end of 2021 Mali brought Russian mercenaries of the **Wagner Group** into the country. Since 2025 the **Africa Corps** of the Russian Ministry of Defence has taken over this role.

Around **Lake Chad**, the terrorist group **Boko Haram** is active, in Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon. In **2014** it kidnapped about 276 schoolgirls in **Chibok** in Nigeria. This sparked the worldwide campaign **“Bring Back Our Girls”**. Many people in the region have had to flee from the violence.

gewusst: The word “Sahel” comes from Arabic and means something like “shore”, meaning the shore of the desert.
In the Sahel, groups linked to al-Qaeda and to the “Islamic State” compete for influence.

teile.einleitung: “Max Havelaar” is first of all a famous novel from the Netherlands. It denounced the exploitation of coffee farmers. Later a fair trade label was named after it, which you can also find in Swiss shops.
wichtigste: The novel “Max Havelaar” was written by Eduard Douwes Dekker under the name Multatuli.
It was published in 1860 and is set on the island of Java.
In 1988 the first Fairtrade label, called Max Havelaar, was launched in the Netherlands.
A Max Havelaar Foundation was set up in Switzerland in 1992.
Migros and Coop took part from the very beginning.
Max Havelaar bananas have been available in Switzerland since 1997.

abschnitte.text: In 1860 the Dutchman **Eduard Douwes Dekker** published the novel **“Max Havelaar”**. He used the pen name **Multatuli**, which means “I have endured much” in Latin. The novel is set on the island of **Java** in the **Dutch East Indies**, today's Indonesia. It describes how the local farmers were oppressed. They had to grow coffee for export instead of enough food for themselves. The book became a classic of Dutch literature.

In 1988 the first **Fairtrade label** was launched in the **Netherlands**, named after the novel. Behind it were the church organisation **Solidaridad** and the priest **Frans van der Hoff**. At first it was about coffee from small farmers in Mexico. The farmers receive a **minimum price** and also a **premium** for community projects. Other countries took up the idea in the following years.

In Switzerland the **Max Havelaar Foundation** was founded in 1992 by several Swiss aid organisations. The federal government paid a start-up grant, but only on one condition: the two largest retailers, **Migros** and **Coop**, had to sell fair products. This way the label quickly reached many shops. After coffee, honey, cocoa, sugar and tea, **bananas** followed in March 1997. They became one of the most successful Fairtrade products in Switzerland.

gewusst: A novel from 1860 gave its name to a modern label more than 120 years later.
In Switzerland fair trade bananas are especially popular; they are among the best-known Fairtrade products in the country.

teile.einleitung: Monaco is a tiny principality on the Mediterranean coast. After Vatican City it is the second-smallest country in the world. It is known for its Formula 1 race, its casino and the princely Grimaldi family.
wichtigste: Monaco is a principality with a prince at its head.
Albert II has been Prince of Monaco since 2005.
The Grimaldi family has ruled for more than 700 years.
Monaco lies on the Mediterranean and on the land side borders only France.
It is only about 2 square kilometres in size.
The Formula 1 Monaco Grand Prix takes place every year.
The official language is French.

abschnitte.titel: A tiny state by the sea
abschnitte.text: Monaco lies on the **Côte d'Azur** on the **Mediterranean**. On the land side it borders only **France**. At about **2 square kilometres** it is one of the smallest countries in the world. Only **Vatican City** is smaller. Because many people live in so little space, there are many tower blocks. Monaco is regarded as the country with the highest population density in the world.

Monaco is a **principality**. At its head is a **prince**. The **Grimaldi** family has ruled the country for more than **700 years**. Since 2005 **Albert II** has been Prince of Monaco. He succeeded his father **Rainier III**, who was married to the American actress Grace Kelly. The prince lives in the **Prince's Palace** on a rock above the harbour.

Every year Monaco hosts the **Monaco Grand Prix**. **Formula 1 cars** race right through the narrow streets of the city. The track runs past houses and the harbour and through a tunnel. Overtaking there is very difficult. The race is regarded as one of the most famous in the world.

The official language in Monaco is **French**. There is also the old national language, **Monégasque**, which can be learned at school. People pay with the **euro**, even though Monaco is not a member of the EU. A well-known district is **Monte Carlo** with its famous casino. The **Oceanographic Museum** with its large aquarium is also worth seeing.

gewusst: Monaco is smaller than many Swiss municipalities, for example smaller than the city of Zurich.
For a long time the Oceanographic Museum in Monaco was directed by the famous ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau.
